common_name: Emperor Daffodil (Historic Backhouse Giant Trumpet Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, choosing a site where the clump can remain undisturbed for years.

directions: Raised by English nurseryman William Backhouse and introduced around 1865, Emperor was bred alongside his bicolor cultivar 'Empress' and ranks among the first giant trumpet daffodils to reach Victorian gardens. Unlike its white-and-yellow sibling, Emperor carries a uniform deep golden-yellow perianth and trumpet of matching shade, giving a bold, self-colored flower on sturdy stems. Its size and vigor helped set the standard for the large-trumpet (Division 1) daffodils that followed, and it is still occasionally offered by heirloom bulb specialists today. Let the foliage die back fully after flowering and divide clumps only when flowering begins to decline.

common_name: Little Gem Daffodil (Miniature Self-Yellow Trumpet Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun, tucked where its small scale will not be lost among larger bulbs.

directions: Little Gem is a long-cultivated miniature Division 1 trumpet daffodil, scaled down to a stature of only four to six inches with proportionally small deep-yellow flowers in which the perianth and trumpet share the same solid gold tone. It stands alongside 'Bagatelle' and 'Wee Bee' as one of the small handful of true miniature trumpets available to gardeners for most of the twentieth century, and it was drawn on repeatedly as parent stock in early miniature daffodil breeding programs. Grow it in a rock garden, trough, or raised bed where taller neighbors will not overwhelm it, and allow the foliage to yellow and collapse naturally before clearing it away.
